newsitem.title: USA: Ice on moon might support space colony - Pentagon.
newsitem.headline: Ice on moon might support space colony - Pentagon.

text.p: A U.S. military spacecraft has found what appears to be "a dirty, dirty lake" of ice on the moon that could one day help support a permanent human space colony, scientists said on Tuesday.
"We think we have found ice. We're not positive," said Dr. Paul Spudis of the Lunar and Planetary Institute at Rice University during a Pentagon briefing on the finding.
"It's not a sheet or a pond. It's not an ice rink on the moon. It's basically ice mixed in to the dirt."
Spudis said the surface might look no different than the rest of the moon but digging would quickly find the ice mixed in, much like on Earth's tundra.
"It's a lake ... a dirty, dirty lake," said Dr. Stewart Nozette of Lawrence Livermore Laboratory.

The moon was thought to be bone dry. The possibility it may hold water deposited by comets that smashed into a deep, dark, extremely cold crater in its South Pole-Aitken Basin turned up in radar soundings from a military research satellite.
Spudis and other scientists estimate that a quarter of a cubic mile of ice has been located and said that alone would would support a manned space station for considerable time.
They said it could be refined into liquid oxygen and hydrogen to fuel rockets as well as provide water and oxygen for a space station in the next 50 years.
Other scientists contacted by Reuters expressed scepticism that ice had been found or, if it had been, that it would have much practical benefits for lunar exploration.
But at the Pentagon briefing, Nozette of the Livermore Laboratory called it "highly likely" ice had been found.
He said what scientists know so far is that radar waves bounced by the military spacecraft Clementine into the crater and back to Earth antennas four times displayed the characteristics of water ice.
Spudis said a Lunar Prospector spacecraft to be launched next October to circle the moon will be able to confirm whether the ice is there or is not.
Some scientists clearly will need more convincing.

"There's a community that's very anxious to talk about going back to moon and living in a colony, they are very passionate about that. One of the keys to that venture is to be able to find water, so those people will be very excited," said John Wood, a scientist at the Harvard-Smithsonian Centre for Astrophysics in Cambridge, Ma.
"Personally, I've always been sceptical of that whole proposition, I think it's a lot of wishful thinking."
But the Defence Department said in a statement issued late Monday that "the discovery of ice on the moon has enormous implications for a permanent human return to the moon."

"This hydrogen and oxygen is a prime rocket fuel, giving the space programme the ability to re-fuel rockets at a lunar 'filling station' and making transport to and from the moon more economical," it said. "Additionally, the water from lunar polar ice and oxygen generated from the ice could support a permanent facility or outpost on the moon."
U.S. Apollo spacecraft teams visited the moon in a series missions from July 1969 to December 1972.
The scientists said the water for the ice probably came to the moon in dirt-ice comets that have slammed into it over the past four billion years.

They said most of the water evaporated in high daytime temperatures. But any vapour that dropped into the polar basin would have been trapped and frozen by near-absolute zero temperatures in the solar system's deepest known crater.

The South Pole-Aitken basin is about 1,500 miles (2,500 kms) in diameter and up to 8 miles (13 km) deep. Pentagon spokesman Rick Lehner said the possible ice-dirt lake is estimated to be about 400 yards (366 metres) long and 16 feet (5 metres) to 33 feet (10 metres) deep.
The Clementine spacecraft is a $75 million programme launched in 1994 that uses the moon as a target to test sensors and other devices for anti-missile missile defences.
